newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FEATURE - Argentina's economic malaise leads to unpopularity.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Argentina's economic malaise leads to unpopularity.

text.p: When one of new Economy Minister Roque Fernandez's aides compared the economy to the Titanic, Fernandez snapped back that Argentina is "a pretty good ship" going through a "small storm".
But with general strikes, disastrous opinion polls and jumpy markets buffeting its bows, the Peronist government is struggling to dispel a certain sinking feeling.
"People are somehow unsatisfied, and the markets are following public opinion," Fernandez acknowledged this week.
That malaise translates into the worst opinion poll result for the Peronists since President Carlos Menem first came to power in 1989.

A Gallup poll published in Pagina 12 newspaper last week showed 70 percent disapproval of both Menem and his economic policies, with eight out of 10 people expressing no faith in the government's ability to solve Argentina's problems.

The words "malestar" and "mal humour" -- bad mood -- have been cropping up everywhere in the declarations of politicians, business leaders and analysts since the launch of Fernandez's tough fiscal austerity package on August 12 and of unpopular benefit cuts by his predecessor Domingo Cavallo in July.
Menem's brother, the powerful Peronist senator Eduardo, this week lamented a "somewhat collective hysteria" gripping a country whose "favourite sport is bashing the government."

One political cartoonist joked that at least it has put a stop to speculation about whether Carlos Menem will try to get reelected for a third consecutive term in 1999, after winning a second term in May 1995 with a landslide 50 percent victory.

Menem, who denies such ambitions, was voted back to power on the widespread belief that only he had the political clout to steer Argentina through tough economic reforms when there is growing demand for populist measures to combat poverty and unemployment, which current runs at 17.1 percent.
FEARS THAT MENEN HAS LOST POWER OVER THE UNIONS

The fear is that Menem has lost that political power -- not least over the unions, who staged a successful 24-hour general strike on August 8 and plan another this month. The main CGT labour federation is now railing against the "neo-liberal economic model" it once supported and the spectacle of union rivalry merely underlines the feeling of growing political instability.

Jorge Di Fiori, head of the Argentine Chamber of Commerce, said shop and service sales have been falling for three weeks "giving daily evidence of a slowdown because of uncertainty, and that uncertainty is political, not economic."

In this climate, the drole observation of Fernandez's aide Guillermo Calvo, an economist famous for forecasting Mexico's Tequila debacle, that "some politicians are playing cards on the deck of the Titanic" did not go down well.

But former Central Bank chief Fernandez, whose appointment to replace Cavallo got an initially warm reception on the hopes it would smoothe relations between the Economy Ministry and Congress, has not found it plain sailing.

Just two weeks after taking over, Fernandez launched a tax package -- including new fuel taxes, spreading value-added tax and slashing tax reimbursements -- aimed at narrowing a budget deficit he said would otherwise hit $6.6 billion by year-end. This bitter pill came on top of Cavallo's reductions in family allowance benefits and in tax breaks for food vouchers.
The measures were welcomed by the International Monetary Fund, which set Argentina a $2.5 billion deficit goal for the whole year but watched it hit that target by mid-year.
AUSTERITY MEASURES ATTACKED BY FISCAL HAWKS AND DOVES

But delays and alterations in Congress mean Fernandez will only make half the $1.2 billion impact on the deficit he hoped for; so he now finds his austerity measures criticised by fiscal hawks and doves alike.
Business leaders, who accept the need for fiscal solvency, are openly anxious that the measures will scupper chances of a recovery from the recession.

"The measures not only don't improve the situation of industry, they mean we are worse off," said Jorge Blanco, chief of the Argentine Industrial Union business lobby, Villegas, a hitherto firm backer of the Menem government.
"The rise in fuel tax and cut in export incentives mean less local consumption and less labour activity, which might be good orthodox practice but do not help the productive sector."

Banco Rio, one of Argentina's top two private banks, was equally critical: "All in all, the fiscal package does not improve substantially fiscal performance and it increases the bad mood in the population. Thus the lack of confidence among investors increases."

Rio predicted that the overall uncertainty could hurt economic activity for the third quarter, while analysts at Macroeconomica forecast that a rise in industrial activity seen in July would not be sustained over the next few months.
As the Peronist majority in Congress prepared this week to start pushing a watered-down version of Fernandez's reforms through Congress, they warned it was his "last blank cheque".
"The government simply cannot win at the moment," said a Bear Stearns research report.

"If the new package is introduced on schedule the economy may be hurt, there are fears of new political turmoil and the market goes down. If the cuts are reduced or delayed, the deficit target is missing again and the market goes down."
